note_tweet.text:
GROK BOT + JEV IS INSANE FOR BUILDING A COMPANY BRAIN

i pulled the whole architecture out of the typesafe and anthropic docs and packed it into a 14-page pdf

the 10 steps:

1. meet the trio
> opus 5.5 thinks, jev decides, grok @bot holds the branch

2. stop asking a text generator for a yes or no
> jev returns a typed answer with a calibrated probability in 0.44s for $0.00035

3. ask everything at once
> choice, score and noul run in parallel, so the fourth question costs almost nothing

4. branch on the number
> 0.999 goes straight into grok bot's if statement. ~99% of turns end right here

5. stop routing blind
> opus 5.5 to sonnet and back costs 5.84 against 3.32 for staying on 5.5

6. keep one context warm
> cache reads at $0.20 per mtok are 20x cheaper than a fresh load

7. escalate the hard part
> grok bot sends the toughest 1% to opus 5.5 with 1m context and 66.4% on terminal-bench 4.0

8. score every chunk on every query
> keep whole, summarize or drop. the context gets rebuilt each turn

9. gate the actual command
> every bash call gets classified before grok bot runs it, inside your own code

10. judge 100% of runs
> $3.50 a day for 10,000 traces, and it matched the human label on all 500 decisions

the result: a while loop that paid a frontier model for every tiny call turns into a brain that spends a fraction of a cent to notice and pays properly only when it has to think

whoever brings this into their team walks into the budget meeting with the ai bill cut and the output up

the pdf maps the company brain. the loop side - how jev takes a claude bill from $765 to $3 a month - is in the article below ↓

note_tweet.text:
Grok Bot is stupidly f*cking good..

easily one of my best discoveries in the last 2 months. I keep handing it tasks I'd normally put off, and now these bots barely leave the sidebar

if I had to start again, these are the first 6 I'd add

01 / Reverse Engineer

I built this to take apart apps, sites, APIs and binaries, then rebuild a version I can run myself, with evidence behind the findings

→ https://t.co/iMA0Eaf6DJ

02 / Research Desk

research crew I set up for keeping project research running 24/7. brings the findings into reports with sources attached, so I can check what it found

→ https://t.co/s2u4G8oX4f

03 / Proto Bot

Shub Gaur at SpaceX Super Intelligence made this one. turns a feature idea into a working prototype inside your app, with a draft PR and video to review

→ https://t.co/CzZ3BepV7r

04 / tinkabot

turns APIs into plugins your agents can use. Lauren Tan at SpaceXSI built it, and it's pretty damn handy when the service you need has no ready-made integration

→ https://t.co/T0RIHSBtzN

05 / Clip Bot

takes long recordings and returns captioned highlights. saves another hour of scrubbing through footage looking for a few usable moments

→ https://t.co/mao6OYKaZW

06 / Outbound Desk

an outreach bot I put together for finding leads and preparing drafts across email, X and LinkedIn. keeps everything in one Google Sheet for review

→ https://t.co/4GIBsNOyju

I'm not even exaggerating, this setup gives me back around 4 hours a day, and being able to use it from my phone makes it so damn convenient

those links are a pretty deep rabbit hole once you start using them

article.plain_text:
Why now
Agents are leaving the chat window and moving into the tools you already use. Gartner expects a third of enterprise apps to ship with agentic AI by 2028, up from under 1% in 2024.
So treat them like a team: ten bots, one job title each, and one approver. You.
How to install a bot
Reply under the post and tag the @bot, or paste its prompt into Grok Bot. It asks its setup questions once, then runs on its own schedule.
10. Personal X Assistant
Your researcher, writer and hook specialist for X. It learns your voice from your last 50 posts, scans 20 accounts you learn from and hands you one queue a day.
Runs: daily at 08:00 · Replaces: a social media assistant · Never: posts for you
 
 
9. Competitor Monitor
It snapshots every rival once, then checks pricing pages, changelogs and job boards against that baseline every day. The weekly report holds only what changed, each line with its source.
Runs: daily check, weekly report · Replaces: a market analyst's weekly · Never: pads a quiet week
 
 
8. Lead List Builder
Every lead comes with a public, dated signal and a link to prove it. No evidence, no row. It stops at 50 and drafts a 4-line opener for the best ones.
Runs: on demand, stops at 50 · Replaces: hours of manual prospecting · Never: guesses emails or sends
 
 
7. Group Chat Manager
Microsoft's 2025 Work Trend Index counts 275 interruptions in an average workday. This bot reads Telegram, Discord, Slack and WhatsApp for you and turns them into two digests.
Runs: digests at 09:00 and 18:00 · Replaces: reading every group chat · Never: sends without you
 
 
6. Subscription Auditor
In a C+R Research survey, people guessed they spend $86 a month on subscriptions. They actually paid $219, and 42% were paying for something they no longer used.
Runs: monthly · Replaces: a yearly money audit · Never: cancels or pays by itself
 
 
5. Content Repurposer
It pulls your outlier posts and rewrites each idea natively for X, LinkedIn, Threads and Instagram, inside each platform's limit.
Runs: weekly · Replaces: a repurposing freelancer · Never: publishes
 
 
4. Morning Brief
McKinsey found that interaction workers spend 28% of the week on email and nearly 20% looking for information. One page at 07:30 takes the first chunk back.
Runs: every day at 07:30 · Replaces: a chief of staff's morning · Never: replies or accepts for you
 
 
3. Grok Swarm
One orchestrator splits your question into tasks, spawns up to 10 specialist bots, runs them in parallel and merges their work into one report. Conflicts are shown, not averaged.
Runs: on demand, up to 10 agents · Replaces: a small research team · Never: hides a disagreement
 
 
2. Build-Anything Agent
Describe a tool in plain words. It asks 5 questions, writes a one-page spec for you to approve, builds on its own cloud machine and shows a real run before it hands anything over.
Runs: on demand · Replaces: a contract developer for small tools · Never: deploys or spends without your OK
 
 
1. Second Brain
Send it anything you save. It reads it in full, links it by idea and brings it back when you work on that topic.
Runs: always on, weekly review · Replaces: a notes system you never update · Never: shares your notes
 
 
 
Where to start
Two bots a week, starting with the ones that give you time back. Tonight: paste bot #4.
4 tips for better output
Show, don't describe. Three posts you like teach a bot your voice faster than a paragraph about it.
One job per bot. Two jobs in one prompt make two worse bots.
Watch the first week. Edit its drafts and tell it why. Add what you learn to the rules tag.
Make your own. Copy any prompt here, keep the tags, change the job.

article.plain_text:
Most developers who try to reverse engineer a compiled binary or an opaque protocol hit the same wall within twenty minutes.
They open a hex editor, drown in an unreadable ocean of assembly, get lost in hundreds of tangled jump instructions, and abandon the project. They do not know which tool loads the target, which command extracts the logic, or how to translate raw machine instructions into software they can cleanly rebuild.
 
When developers try to solve this with standard AI chatbots, they run into a different bottleneck. Traditional chat models cannot run disassemblers, execute debuggers, or inspect live network traffic. They truncate long outputs, hallucinate struct layouts, and stop running the second you close your laptop.
 
The breakthrough combination in 2026 is pairing REA with Grok Bot.
 
At the center of this workflow is morluto/rea (Reverse Engineer Anything): the open-source Model Context Protocol (MCP) toolkit that crossed 110,000 GitHub stars by turning AI coding agents into autonomous reverse-engineering machines. REA connects models directly to native disassembly engines (Ghidra, Hopper, IDA), JavaScript and Electron AST analyzers, and network inspection bridges.
 
 
However, running REA purely on a local laptop comes with severe friction: multi-gigabyte analysis caches, heavy Java runtimes, and the inability to let an agent decompile large codebases overnight while your machine sleeps.
This is where Grok Bot comes in.
By deploying REA inside Grok Bot's dedicated cloud Linux computer, you give the agent its own bash terminal, persistent filesystem, and 24/7 background runtime in the data center. The agent drives REA autonomously, testing hypotheses, decompiling hot functions, and extracting clean behavioral specifications without touching your local machine.
 
Reverse engineering is not about piracy or cracking. It is about deep interoperability: understanding how sealed software, proprietary file formats, and closed protocols work so you can engineer superior, clean-room, open-source alternatives (the exact methodology the WordCraft team used to clean-room rebuild office suites in pure Rust).
 
This 8-module course walks through the complete methodology: from mounting REA inside a persistent cloud environment to producing verified clean-room specifications and shipping production rebuilds.
For developers who want an immediate shortcut, you can also launch the pre-configured xAI Bot template:
→ Optional: Clone the Reverse Engineering Bot Template (Contains pre-baked REA guidelines and sandbox boundary rules).
 
Module 01: The REA Engine in a Cloud Container
To understand why this architecture works, you must look at how REA bridges the gap between language models and raw binaries.
An LLM on its own cannot disassemble machine code. It reads text and writes text. morluto/rea acts as the specialized MCP translation layer sitting between the model and the disassembly engines:
It loads targets into real disassemblers (Ghidra, Hopper, IDA, Rizin) or JavaScript AST analyzers.
It exposes findings as structured, callable MCP tools (rea_analyze_binary, rea_extract_strings, rea_get_pseudocode).
It enforces evidence-backed reasoning: every observation returned to the model includes exact memory offsets, raw bytes, call sites, and pseudocode cross-references.
 
 
Why Run REA Inside Grok Bot?
Running REA on a local laptop works, but it ties up your CPU, requires keeping your computer open, and risks executing untrusted targets on your primary development machine.
Hosting REA inside Grok Bot's dedicated virtual machine solves this:
Zero Host Risk: Untrusted binaries, malware samples, and proprietary executables are inspected inside an ephemeral cloud container.
Persistent 24/7 Execution: Grok Bot keeps analyzing, disassembling, and fuzzing even after you shut your laptop lid.
Multi-Gigabyte Memory Offloading: Ghidra projects and AST symbol trees remain in the cloud filesystem (~/workspace/), keeping your local environment completely clean.
 
 
Module 02: Provisioning the Environment (REA Setup & Bot Charter)
Setting up the REA engine inside Grok Bot takes less than two minutes via the standard package runner.
Step 1: Install Dependencies in the Cloud Terminal
Open your Grok Bot terminal and install the prerequisites (Node.js 22+, Python, and your preferred disassembler):
 
Step 2: Register REA via NPM
Run the official REA setup command from morluto/rea:
 
The installer detects available runtimes, registers the REA MCP server, and generates matching workflow instructions.
To optimize context window usage on long decompilation traces, REA defaults to compact schemas. If your bot needs complete parameter descriptions, pass the environment variable:
 
(Note: If you prefer to bypass manual setup, the pre-built x.ai Reverse Engineering Bot Template already has these MCP tools and analysis prompts pre-configured).
 
Step 3: Establish the Bot Charter
Define clear operational boundaries in the bot's system instructions:
 
 
 
Module 03: The Universal Target Router
The single biggest mistake in reverse engineering is opening a heavy disassembler when the target application is an Electron wrapper, a packaged Python script, or a managed .NET assembly.
REA incorporates an automated target router. Instruct your bot to classify the target before opening any disassembly session:
 
How REA Routes Your Targets:
 
If REA detects an Electron app (like Slack, Notion, or 1Password), it skips native disassembly entirely. It extracts the app.asar archive, parses the internal modules, maps the IPC communication boundaries between the main and renderer processes, and gives you the exact JavaScript logic in seconds.
 
 
 
Module 04: Automated Recon & Cross-Reference Mapping
Never decompile an entire binary blindly. Modern production binaries contain thousands of functions; dumping all of them into an LLM context will drown the model in noise and deplete your token budget.
Instead, instruct Grok Bot to perform surface reconnaissance using REA:
 
The Power of Cross-Reference (Xref) Triage
In any compiled binary:
A function with 150+ cross-references is a core architectural primitive (e.g., memory allocator, custom packet serializer, authentication validator).
A function with 1–2 cross-references is usually initialization boilerplate or a peripheral helper.
REA maps the xref counts across the entire binary. By instructing Grok Bot to focus its decompilation efforts exclusively on the top 5% of functions with the highest xref density, you decode the core logic of the application in hours instead of weeks.
 
 
Module 05: Evidence-Based Decompilation & Semantic Reconstruction
Once the high-priority function offsets are isolated, Grok Bot uses REA to extract decompiled C pseudocode.
Inside the cloud container, REA queries the backend disassembler (Ghidra, Hopper, or IDA) and returns the pseudocode alongside its structural metadata:
 
 
Decompiler output is naturally obfuscated by register re-use and missing headers (var_28h, arg_8, cryptic bitwise shifts).
Because Grok Bot has access to REA's full evidence trail, you run a semantic reconstruction prompt:
 
REA guarantees that the model does not hallucinate: every reconstructed variable is mapped directly to a specific stack offset or register recorded in the disassembler's database.
 
Module 06: Conquering Obfuscation & Dynamic Verification
Commercial targets often deploy anti-analysis techniques: string encryption tables, dead code injection, and control flow flattening (massive switch dispatchers inside infinite loops).
REA and Grok Bot handle obfuscated targets using a complementary static-dynamic workflow:
1. Semantic Pruning
REA strips dead branches, constant-condition jumps (if (1 == 1)), and compiler-inserted stack canaries before passing pseudocode to the LLM, reducing analysis payload sizes by up to 75%.
2. Sandbox Dynamic Tracing
When static analysis cannot resolve an encrypted payload or dynamically resolved API import, Grok Bot leverages its cloud terminal to trace the process live:
 
Because execution happens entirely inside xAI's data center container, you can safely trace unknown binaries without exposing your local operating system or network perimeter.
 
 
Module 07: The Multi-Bot Swarm & Clean-Room Protocol
Analyzing a complex enterprise binary requires dividing labor. A single bot thread that attempts to decompile 500 functions will inevitably suffer from context rot, confusing struct offsets and contradicting its own findings.
Grok Bot allows you to spin up a team of specialized bots sharing the same cloud workspace:
 
 
The Four Inviolable Laws of Clean-Room Engineering
To ensure your rebuild is 100% legally sound and free of proprietary copyright infringement:
Observe Behavior, Never Copy Code: Treat the original binary as a sealed black box. Document inputs, outputs, and side effects. Never copy decompiled C pseudocode into your production repo.
Specs Over Sources: Protocol schemas and data formats must be documented in vendor-neutral specifications (e.g., Kaitai Struct, Protobuf, or RFC-style Markdown).
Strict Context Isolation: The bot that implements the new software must never read the disassembled code. It works strictly from the clean specification produced by the analysis bot.
Original Asset Pipeline: Every UI component, icon, sound effect, and font must be generated from scratch or drawn from open-source repositories with clean license attribution.
 
Module 08: Rebuilding, Differential Parity Fuzzing & Exposing MCP
With the behavioral specification verified, your Clean-Room Coder Bot builds the native replacement.
Because you are writing a fresh implementation, you do not inherit thirty years of legacy baggage. You can replace bloated, single-threaded C++ or heavy Electron wrappers with a blazing-fast, memory-safe architecture in Rust, Go, or modern TypeScript.
 
Proving Parity with Differential Fuzzing
How do you prove your clean-room rebuild matches the closed original?
You run automated differential testing inside Grok Bot's container:
 
If both systems produce byte-identical responses across 10,000 edge-case vectors, you have mathematically demonstrated behavioral parity.
Exposing Your Rebuild via MCP
The ultimate destination for any reverse-engineered tool in 2026 is the Model Context Protocol (MCP).
Wrap your new clean-room engine as a lightweight MCP server:
Expose its internal functions as callable tools for other AI agents.
Provide typed JSON schemas for all inputs and parameters.
Package the binary for one-line installation (cargo install or npm install -g).
Now, you have not only replaced closed software with an open, high-performance alternative, but your entire agent fleet can programmatically command it.
 
 
Six Costly Traps That Waste a Weekend
Disassembling an Electron App: If the target contains an app.asar archive, never open Ghidra. Use REA's analyze-javascript-application to inspect the source JavaScript directly.
Analyzing Functions Sequentially: Do not start at memory address 0x00401000. Sort functions by REA xref counts and begin with the top 5% core dispatchers.
Running Binaries on Your Host Machine: Always let Grok Bot execute untrusted code inside its isolated cloud container with restricted network namespaces.
Getting Stuck in Obfuscation Traps: If an obscure helper function is heavily virtualized, treat it as a black box. Isolate its inputs and outputs at the call boundary and move on.
Breaching Clean-Room Separation: Never let your coding bot inspect raw decompilation logs. Enforce strict isolation: Analysis Bot writes specs, Coder Bot implements specs.
Shipping Without Differential Fuzzing: A single successful test run does not guarantee compatibility. Run thousands of automated test cases before tagging a release.
 
Conclusion: Stop Prompting. Start Rebuilding.
Reverse engineering is no longer an art reserved for a handful of assembly veterans.
By combining the specialized tooling of morluto/rea with the 24/7 autonomous cloud container of Grok Bot, you possess an unkillable reverse-engineering pipeline:
An agent that doesn't just chat, but executes real tools in an operating system.
Evidence-backed decompilation with exact memory addresses and xref graphs.
True clean-room reconstruction that produces 100% legal, high-performance open-source software.
Eight modules. One persistent cloud machine. Zero copied code.
 
Use Reverse Engineering Bot Template

article.plain_text:
You check every step your agents take. Not because you want to, but because nothing else does.
Getting out of that chair takes two things, and almost everyone builds only one of them.
A loop makes a unit of work correct without you. A graph decides which units exist at all.
Here is the split, the mechanics that are not obvious, and the point where you approve one thing instead of everything.
 
A loop is a check that can fail
Strip everything else away and a loop is four parts: produce, check, correct, repeat until green.
The check is the whole thing.
Without something that can fail the work while you are out of the room, you do not have a loop. You have a scheduler.
This sounds obvious and almost nobody writes the check first.
They build the work, then bolt a review onto the end, and the review is another model asked to look at the output.
Two optimists agreeing.
Write the condition first, and write it so a program could evaluate it:
 
 
That last one catches careful people. Absence of an error is not evidence of correctness.
Build a loop on it and you get a system that confidently repeats a mistake until the budget runs out, with a clean log the whole way.
 
The ceiling nobody warns you about
A loop makes one unit of work better. That is its entire job, and it is very good at it.
It cannot decide which units exist, or their order, or notice that two of the five steps never needed to wait for each other.
So you get a very good agent running the wrong three steps, in the wrong order, one at a time.
Every step is correct. The result is still slow and still wrong-shaped, and tuning the loop will not fix it, because the fault is not inside any unit.
That is the moment people blame the model. It is also the moment the next layer starts paying for itself.
 
The graph is the layer above
A graph is the shape of the work: what runs, what runs at the same time, what waits, what never runs at all, and where results go back.
Two things and nothing else. A node is a unit of work: one bounded job, one input in, one output out.
An edge is a dependency, this node's output feeds that node's input.
The mistake behind every unnecessary wait is treating "and then" as an edge.
Summarize the file and then check the weather has no edge between them. The weather does not consume the summary.
Those are two independent nodes that a linear script chained, and the chaining came from the order you typed them.
So run this on every arrow in a pipeline you already have: does the next step actually read the previous step's output?
If you cannot name the variable that crosses, there is no edge, and the wait is pure waste.
Most chains have two or three arrows like that, and finding them is usually the largest single speedup available.
The full breakdown of all five layers, in the order they matter, is here: agent-layers.vercel.app
Four kinds of node, and one of them is not a model
Splitter, worker, code node, gate. That is the whole vocabulary.
The splitter cuts the work into units and sits at the front.
It decides more than any other node, because splitting by the wrong dimension wastes everything downstream.
Cut a repository by folder and four workers audit the same three files.
Cut by blast radius and each one sees something the others cannot.
Workers do one unit each, with one lens, in their own context. That last part gets skipped constantly.
Give four auditors a shared window and they converge: the first writes a finding, the rest read it, and all four reports centre on the same thing.
You paid four times for one opinion with three echoes.
The code node is the one people forget exists. Merging, ranking, deduplicating, comparing every export before and after.
None of that is reasoning. Each has exactly one correct answer, each is a few lines of code, and running it through a model adds cost, latency and variance to a step that had none.
If you can describe the transformation without using the words judge, decide, assess or summarize, it is code.
A graph where every edge is an agent pays rent on its own wiring.
 
Where the loop actually lives
One sentence resolves the whole confusion. The loop lives inside a node. The graph lives between them.
Inside one unit: produce, check, correct, repeat until green.
Between units: split, fan out, merge, gate, send back. None of the second list is expressible from inside a single unit.
So you do not choose. A graph without loops in its nodes produces unverified work in parallel, which is worse than serially because there is more of it.
A loop without a graph around it is one very good step in a queue nobody designed.
The two return paths, and the one everyone skips
A graph without a way back is a pipeline. It produces output and forgets.
Next week it starts from the same place with the same blind spots.
Working graphs have two return paths, doing different jobs.
The correction edge is short. A gate rejects one unit back to the step that produced it, and it fixes the run you are in.
The learning edge is long. An accepted result goes back to the splitter as a constraint, and it fixes every run after.
Almost everyone builds the first and skips the second. The tell is a system that is fast and never gets smarter.
The learning edge does not carry the output, it carries a constraint derived from it:
 
Notice where it lands. Not in the worker's instructions, in the brief that shapes how the work gets cut.
A confirmed cause becomes a rule, so the next break starts where this one ended.
 
Return the unit, not the batch
This is the most expensive mistake on the return path, and it is worth stating plainly.
Four slices were ported. One fails its tests. If the whole batch goes back, three correct slices get rewritten.
Their next version is different, not better, because nothing was wrong with them.
Now you re-verify all four, and any of the three may fail this time for unrelated reasons.
You converted one failure into four uncertain outcomes and paid for the privilege. Do it twice in a run and it never converges.
From the outside this looks like the model failing repeatedly. It is a return path destroying correct work.
Four things travel with a return, and each is doing a job:
 
The scope line matters more than it looks.
Without it a returned unit grows: the agent opens the file, notices two adjacent issues, fixes those too, and your one-slice correction becomes a four-file diff nobody reviewed.
Cap it at three attempts. If a unit fails three corrections the problem is in the plan that produced it, and the loop cannot see the plan.
 
Open the gate on blast radius, not on confidence
Most write-ups build a confidence score, set a threshold, and let anything above it through. That is the wrong variable.
Confidence is the weakest input in that decision, for a reason that is easy to miss: it is the only one the model can influence.
The strong variable is what happens if the change is wrong. Sort work by how expensive the mistake is to undo:
Reversible and contained. A copy change, a test, an isolated function with coverage. One bad merge costs a revert, so this lane can open first.
Reversible but wide. A shared utility, a schema addition, anything a dozen callers touch. Gate on deterministic checks plus a clean trajectory.
Hard to reverse. Migrations, deletions, anything writing to production data or moving money. This lane does not open, regardless of score.
That third row is not a threshold set very high. It is a lane that does not open, and the distinction matters because thresholds get adjusted and closed lanes do not.
Inside an open lane the gate reads evidence in order: deterministic results, then the trajectory of this run, then how often work from this node has been rolled back before, and the model's own assessment last.
 
Where to start on your own work
Take one thing you do repeatedly. Draw the splitter, the lanes, the merge, one gate, one back edge.
Build the gate first. Everything gets easier once something can fail loudly, and a graph without a gate is just a faster way to produce unverified output.
Then the lanes. Then the learning edge, last, because you cannot derive constraints from accepted results until something is accepting results.
Put the human on one step, at the point of highest consequence and lowest reversibility.
Approve the merge. Choose which fixes ship. Not reviewing intermediate output, not confirming each step.
A human in the middle of a graph becomes the slowest node in it, and the graph runs exactly as fast as a person reading things.
I put all five layers into a full course, twenty lessons with the templates, the configs and the order to build them in: agent-layers.vercel.app
Three lines hold the whole discipline. Measure the path, not only the answer it landed on.
A verdict that does not change what runs next is a report.
And any failure you do not turn into a permanent constraint, you will meet again.
Most people will keep tuning one loop and calling it a system.
The ones who draw the graph around it will run a fleet, and never quite understand why everyone else finds it so hard to keep up.
 
If you want the one-page version of the graph layer before anything else, DM me the word Graph.
Also follow me for more on agent internals, and subscribe to my Telegram channel:
https://t.me/+75nMf005jRpjMDU1
